extracted.intended_audience: crime-fiction writers, readers, and genre-interested bloggers/aspiring authors
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and applying the distinguishing characteristics, tropes, tone, and historical roots that separate hardboiled crime fiction from noir (and how to slot a piece as one or the other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of darkness / bleakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled is dark; noir is much darker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explicitly: 'hardboiled is dark and noir is much darker.' Further wording: 'Noir is dark and grim. Noir is urban gothic—hopeless.' Use the relative scale of darkness to decide sub-genre placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall tone: hopelessness vs gritty unsentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir emphasizes hopelessness and an urban-gothic mood; hardboiled is gritty and unsentimental but can allow for some restoration of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post: 'Noir is urban gothic—hopeless. Hardboiled is gritty and unsentimental.' Use mood (hopeless vs pragmatic grit) as a core classifier; examples given: 'Breaking Bad' as noir, 'Law and Order' as modern hardboiled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist moral positioning / role
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled protagonists act as a 'white knight' in a corrupt world; noir protagonists are themselves part of the scummy world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quote: 'The protagonist in noir must himself (herself) be part of the scummy world. The protagonist in hardboiled is a white knight in a world of scum.' Evaluate whether your protagonist is an outsider trying to do right or embedded in corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral clarity vs ambiguity and final outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled tends toward a protagonist who 'has done the right thing' and some order is restored; noir presents blurred right/wrong where moral clarity may be unattainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Megan Abbott quote: hardboiled endings — 'the hero has done the right thing, or close to it, and order, to a certain extent, has been restored.' Noir — 'everyone is fallen, and right and wrong are not clearly defined and maybe not even attainable.' Use the ending and moral resolution as a diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological instability of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir focuses on psychological instability in people and institutions; protagonists may be dangerously unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post: 'Noir crime writing examines psychological instability in people and their institutions. Being dangerously unstable is the key characteristic of noir protagonists.' If your work foregrounds inner breakdown and institutional rot, it leans noir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and atmosphere (urban, rainy, gothic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled historically set on perpetually-rainy, mean American city streets; noir is urban-gothic and hopeless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery to include: 'mean streets,' rain-sodden cities, low-rent districts, Venetian-blind-lit offices. Use a strongly urban, atmospheric setting to anchor either sub-genre; noir emphasizes gothic hopelessness, hardboiled emphasizes gritty city realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist archetype and pulp tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled staples: the loner detective with a fedora and trench coat, oak-desked office, chain-smoking, a bottle of Scotch, rebel gumshoe with a moral code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post lists conventional hardboiled tropes and slang ('dames' for women, 'gams' for legs, and 'gat' for his gun). Employing or subverting these archetypes signals hardboiled lineage (Black Mask, Hammett, Chandler, Spillane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue and diction (terse, slang-infused)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled prose often uses terse, nuanced dialogue and period slang; contemporary writers cited for dialogue mastery (Elmore Leonard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes: 'Netflix writers now idolize Elmore Leonard as the dialogue man.' Use clipped, idiomatic speech and period slang to evoke a hardboiled voice; noir may use language to reveal psychological interiority rather than punchy repartee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot emphasis: action-facing vs psychological/tragic
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled resembles an action movie with a character-driven plot where the protagonist 'triumphs as best as they can'; noir often centers on tragic or psychologically-driven narratives where triumph may be impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the post: 'Hardboiled is more like an action movie with a character-driven plot where the protagonist triumphs as best as they can.' Consider whether plot momentum is external/action-oriented or internal/psychological to categorize the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of violence, tragedy, and gore
rubrics_metrics.description: Both sub-genres tolerate violence, but the author notes 'my stuff was tragic and gore,' implying violent, tragic content is common and can push tone toward noir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence and presentation of death, gore, and tragic outcomes as indicators: graphic, nihilistic treatment leans noir; gritty but procedural violence with codes of conduct may read as hardboiled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical lineage and period influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardboiled grew from 19th-century wild-west and 1920s American pulp (Black Mask, Hammett, Chandler); noir thrived in the 1940s and resurged during times of social disillusionment (Vietnam, Watergate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post situates genre historically (Pinkerton detective influence, Black Mask, Chandler, Hammett; noir's prominence after the Great Depression and war). Use period references, stylistic lineage, and pulp conventions to anchor authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic concern: institutional critique and societal distrust
rubrics_metrics.description: Noir speaks to periods when authority structures no longer make sense and questions why we should abide by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Noir speaks to us powerfully right now when certain structures of authority no longer make sense. We wonder, ‘Why should we abide by them?’' If your work foregrounds distrust of institutions and systemic rot, it leans noir.
